content: Port-wine stains are congenital vascular malformations of the skin, presenting as flat, red marks during infancy. These lesions do not resolve spontaneously and, if left untreated, may darken and thicken over time, particularly in adulthood. Various laser and light-based therapies are available for treating port-wine stains, but the abundance of options complicates the decision-making process regarding the most effective treatment modality. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate participant satisfaction, clinical efficacy, and adverse effects associated with the use of lasers and light sources for treating port-wine stains. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to April 2010. Additionally, online trial registries were reviewed, and trial authors were contacted when necessary. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized clinical trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of lasers or light sources for treating port-wine stains. The study included five RCTs with a total of 103 participants. All trials employed a within-participant design, and the pulsed dye laser was used in all comparisons. However, the interventions and outcomes were too heterogeneous to allow for statistical pooling of data. Notably, none of the studies directly assessed participant satisfaction, which was a primary outcome of interest. Instead, participant preference was evaluated in three of the five studies. Participants generally preferred the pulsed dye laser over intense pulsed light due to its superior clinical effects. Additionally, the Neodymium:YAG (Nd:YAG) laser was marginally preferred over the pulsed dye laser because it caused shorter-lasting purpura. Furthermore, the combination of the pulsed dye laser with cooling was favored over the pulsed dye laser alone. All trials assessed short-term efficacy, defined as outcomes measured within six months of treatment. The pulsed dye laser demonstrated a reduction in redness of more than 25% in 50% to 100% of participants after one to three treatment sessions, with follow-up periods ranging from four to six months. The efficacy of intense pulsed light and the Nd:YAG laser was evaluated in only one study each. Regarding adverse effects, two trials reported no long-term adverse effects six months post-treatment. However, three trials documented pigmentary changes in 3% to 24% of participants, with the highest incidence observed in Chinese participants with darker skin types. In one study, a participant experienced skin scarring due to an excessively high laser dose. Short-term side effects, including pain, crusting, and blistering, were commonly reported within the first two weeks following treatment. In conclusion, the pulsed dye laser is effective in achieving clinically significant clearance of port-wine stains. However, the evidence for the efficacy of intense pulsed light and other laser types is limited due to the small number of RCTs. High-quality RCTs are necessary to further evaluate the efficacy of different laser and light-based treatments and to assess participant satisfaction comprehensively.
